uncited: Neural volume rendering synthesizes novel views of a scene by optimizing a continuous 5D function (spatial location and viewing direction) to predict volume density and view-dependent color [S1].
It solves the view synthesis problem by replacing explicit geometric representations (like meshes or voxel grids) with a neural network that acts as the volume representation [S1].

Unlike traditional direct volume ray casting which samples a discrete 3D texture, this method queries a coordinate-based Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) or a discrete voxel grid of features along camera rays [S1][S3, unofficial].

It sets itself apart from siblings like [Direct Volume Rendering](1184-direct-volume-rendering.md) by learning the appearance and geometry implicitly from images, enabling high-fidelity reconstruction from sparse input views [S1].
The method relies on the volume rendering integral, discretized into a summation over sample points along a ray [S3, S5, unofficial].
The ray $r$ is parameterized by $r(t) = O + tD$, entering the volume at $t_{start}$ and exiting at $t_{end}$ [Volume Raycasting Discretization](831-volume-raycasting-discretization.md).
The data model is sampled using $s(t)$ [Volume Raycasting Discretization](831-volume-raycasting-discretization.md).
The compositing is performed front-to-back [S2, S3, S8, S9, S11, S14, S16, S20, S23, S26, unofficial].
Let $C'_i$ be the accumulated color and $\alpha'_i$ be the accumulated opacity after sample $i$, with initial conditions $C'_0 = 0$ and $\alpha'_0 = 0$ [S9, unofficial].
Sample the volume at the current ray position to get a scalar value $d_i$ [S2, S5, unofficial].
Apply a transfer function to map the scalar value to color $C_i$ and opacity $\alpha_i$ [S2, S5, unofficial].
If $\alpha' \ge 1$ or a threshold (typically 0.99) [S2, S18, unofficial], terminate the ray (early ray termination) [S2, S3, S4, unofficial].
Rays are cast from the eyepoint, one for each pixel [S1][S4, unofficial].
The volume is typically represented as a 3D texture [S4, S3, unofficial].
Gradients for shading are calculated using a central difference operator [S6, unofficial].
To avoid normal discontinuities that cause visible rings on smooth surfaces, the gradient is computed using a two-voxel offset rather than a one-voxel offset [S18, unofficial].
Sampling is performed using trilinear interpolation [S1][S5, unofficial].
A fixed random offset is applied to each ray's start position to prevent sample layers from appearing as bands [S18, unofficial].
The final accumulated color is typically corrected with gamma 2.2 [S9, unofficial].
Originating from the work on Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [S1], this family of methods represents a shift from explicit to implicit scene representations.
The core idea is to learn a continuous function that maps 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color and density.
This allows for high-quality novel view synthesis from a set of input images without requiring explicit mesh reconstruction or voxelization [S1].
The approach has been extended to various domains, including dynamic scenes, large-scale environments, and differentiable rendering pipelines [S3, unofficial].
